blindSummary:
This country is in a fast-improving transition following a change of government. The most acute traveler-facing risk — the 2025 pride ban, with facial-recognition identification of attendees — has stopped: the 2026 pride march in the capital was held freely. The main opposition party won a supermajority in April 2026, ending 16 years of the previous ruling party's government, and the top court of the supranational union this country belongs to has ruled that its 2021 law restricting "promotion" of homosexuality and gender change to under-18s breaches the union's founding values (handing the new government a repeal mandate).

However, the old government's laws remain on the books: a total ban on domestic legal gender recognition (2020), the 2021 content law, and a constitutional amendment banning LGBTQ public events. The structural weakness that has not changed with the election is detention: a court abroad blocked the extradition of a non-binary person to this country in 2025 because of prison conditions and the person's identity, and watchdogs report transphobia in prisons with a culture of silence.

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation of trans identity, and entry through the region's visa-free travel area poses no trans-specific friction. Social hostility lingers outside the capital, but the state-led demonization that characterised the previous government's years has ended.
blindOutOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying foreign-broadcaster piece (June 2026) covers LGBTQ rights in this country after the election - advocates say they are 'very hopeful' that changes will be made.
A newswire report (Jun 2026): tens of thousands march in this country's capital in the first pride parade since the previous government was voted out, after years of anti-LGBT legislation under it.

Legal-analysis outlet (April 2026): what this country's election (an opposition party's 138 seats, ending the previous ruling party's hold on power) actually means for LGBTQ people - a return to democratic baseline, not liberation. Details a 'constitutional architecture of erasure': the May 2020 total ban on legal gender recognition, enacted by redefining the constitutional term for sex as immutable biological sex, forcing trans citizens to carry mismatched documents.

Encyclopedia overview: same-sex activity legal since 1961; legal gender change de facto impossible since 2018 and explicitly illegal since 2020; a 2021 law restricts 'promotion' of homosexuality or gender change to under-18s; the 2025 pride ban; discrimination protections and public opinion.

A foreign public broadcaster (April 2026): the top court of the supranational union this country belongs to ruled that its anti-LGBTQ laws - the 2021 'promotion' ban reaching under-18s - violate union rules and, unprecedentedly, the union's founding values; the law stigmatised trans and non-heterosexual people by associating them with paedophilia. The ruling came nine days after the country voted to end the previous government's rule.

Queer news outlet (April 2026): a spokesperson for the capital's pride organisation says anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds majority; the new governing party's 138 seats give it that power, but its silence on LGBTQ+ rights raises questions; the most urgent issue is restoring the right of assembly (after the 2025 pride ban). Recaps the 2012 two-sex constitutional amendment, the 2020 adoption ban, and the 2021 law conflating LGBTQ+ people with child abusers.
NOTE: this is a foreign constitutional court's press release (2025), not about this country; it appears to have been included in the source list in error or as comparative context.

A national human-rights committee and a trans advocacy society's joint country report (2025) on LGBTIQ detainees, part of a union-funded project on strengthening the rights of LGBTIQ detainees - the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in this country's detention amid the current legal and political climate.

International human-rights organisation's 2025 world-report chapter on this country: the government's assault on rule of law continued in 2024, including a law giving a government-appointed body broad powers to harass civil society and independent media; includes a sexual-orientation and gender-identity section.

Supranational-union court judgment of 13 March 2025: on the accuracy and rectification of gender-identity data in this country's public registers under the union's data-protection rules - the court addressed the administrative practice of demanding proof of gender-reassignment surgery before correcting data that was incorrect from the time of inclusion.

News outlet feature (April 2020): this country's new law will end legal gender recognition - trans residents speak out as the decree banning gender changes is published; one trans woman called it 'just horrible' and said she did not want to lose good people because of it.
blindLocalsOnly: The 2020 total ban on domestic legal gender recognition is resident-facing; the prison culture of silence affects resident detainees.
